Shoulder shrugging up: set the shoulder blade down and back before each rep.
Injured hand gripping the seat or the other handle: rest it in your lap and keep it open.
arm_safety: Sit down and stand up using your legs; adjust the seat and pin with your uninjured hand (ask staff if a lever is stiff). If the two handles are linked, the unused one may move, so keep your injured arm well clear of it. Injured hand stays open and relaxed in your lap (or the arm in its sling if you still wear one); if you notice it clenching or bracing, reduce the weight. Moderate effort (RIR 2–3) and no breath-holding. Anything your physio prescribes or restricts takes priority. Stop if your injured arm aches, throbs, swells, tingles or goes numb, or you notice any red-flag symptom.

name: Single-arm seated cable row (good arm)
equipment: cable machine or seated row station
why: Builds your upper back, the posture muscles that carry a rucksack well, while the one-sided pull trains your core to resist twisting. It also adds to the cross-education effect for the healing arm.
setup: Only once your clinic or physio has cleared you to train your uninjured arm.
Clip a single D-handle to the low cable (or seated row station) with your uninjured hand and set a light weight.
Sit on the seat or a bench with your feet braced on the footplate or floor, knees soft.
Lean forward to take the handle with your uninjured hand, then sit up tall. Injured arm resting on your thigh or across your stomach.
cues: Sit tall, chest up; no rocking
Pull your elbow back past your ribs, leading with the shoulder blade
Squeeze 1 s, then let the arm reach forward slowly
Shoulders stay square; resist the twist
Breathe out as you pull
mistakes: Leaning back and rocking to move the weight: lighter load, still trunk.
Twisting towards the working side: keep your chest facing forward.
Shrugging: keep the shoulder down, away from your ear.
arm_safety: Seated with your feet braced, so your balance is secure. To finish, let the handle travel forward under control until the stack rests, then let go; never let it snap back. Sit and stand using your legs only. Injured hand open and relaxed on your thigh, well away from the cable (or the arm in its sling if you still wear one). Moderate effort (RIR 2–3) and no breath-holding. Physio instructions take priority. Stop if your injured arm aches, throbs, swells, tingles or goes numb, or you notice any red-flag symptom.

name: Single-arm lat pulldown (good arm)
equipment: lat pulldown machine or high cable
why: Your lats are among the biggest upper-body muscles, so they matter for the +5 kg goal and for future pull-ups, carries and scrambling. Training one side now keeps the pattern and strength alive until both arms can pull.
setup: Only once your clinic or physio has cleared you to train your uninjured arm.
Swap the bar for a single D-handle (uninjured hand, or ask staff) and set a light weight.
Set the thigh pad with your uninjured hand so it sits snugly on your thighs.
Stand, take the handle with your uninjured hand, then sit down under the pad, letting the arm stretch overhead. Injured arm resting on your thigh.
cues: Start each rep by drawing the shoulder blade down
Drive the elbow down towards your back pocket
Handle finishes by your shoulder or upper chest
Return slowly over 2–3 s until the arm is long
Stay upright; breathe out as you pull
mistakes: Leaning far back or bending sideways: lighter weight, ribs down.
Pulling with the hand and biceps only: think 'elbow down', not 'hand down'.
Letting the handle snap up: control the return every rep.
arm_safety: Use a weight light enough that sitting down and standing up with the handle is fully controlled. To finish, stand up slowly so the handle rises until the stack rests, then let go. If the handle is out of reach when seated, use a high cable and a bench instead, or ask staff to pass it to you. Injured arm resting on your thigh, hand relaxed and well clear of the pad and cable (or in its sling if you still wear one). Moderate effort (RIR 2–3) and no breath-holding. Physio instructions take priority. Stop if your injured arm aches, throbs, swells, tingles or goes numb, or you notice any red-flag symptom.

name: Seated dumbbell curl (good arm)
why: Builds the elbow flexors and forearm of your uninjured arm, which are part of carrying and farmer strength, and supports the cross-education effect for the healing arm. Sitting with back support keeps you stable and honest.
setup: Only once your clinic or physio has cleared you to train your uninjured arm.
Set an adjustable bench upright (75–90°) near the dumbbell rack.
Take a light dumbbell from the rack with your uninjured hand, holding it close to your body, and sit down.
Back against the pad, feet flat; injured arm resting on its own thigh.
cues: Elbow stays by your side
Curl up, turning the palm to face you
Squeeze 1 s at the top
Lower over 3 s to a straight arm
Breathe out as you curl
mistakes: Swinging your body: sit back against the pad and lighten the weight.
Elbow drifting forward: keep it pinned by your side.
Half reps: lower all the way down.
arm_safety: Pick up and return the dumbbell with your uninjured hand only, from a rack at hip height where possible rather than the floor. Never pass the dumbbell across your body or near your injured arm. Injured arm resting on its own thigh, hand relaxed (or in its sling if you still wear one). Moderate effort (RIR 2–3) and no breath-holding. Physio instructions take priority. Stop if your injured arm aches, throbs, swells, tingles or goes numb, or you notice any red-flag symptom.

name: Single-arm triceps pushdown (good arm)
why: Your triceps make up much of your upper-arm size and will power every press, push-up and pole plant later. This keeps your uninjured arm strong and adds to the cross-education effect.
setup: Only once your clinic or physio has cleared you to train your uninjured arm.
Pulley at the top; clip on a single D-handle with your uninjured hand and set a light weight.
Stand close to the machine in a short split stance, or sit on a bench under the pulley if you feel at all unsteady.
Elbow tucked by your side; injured arm across your stomach.
cues: Upper arm stays still, pinned to your side
Push down until the elbow is straight and squeeze 1 s
Let the forearm come back up to about 90°, slowly
Stand tall; don't lean over the handle
Breathe out as you push
mistakes: Elbow flaring or drifting forward: lighter weight, elbow glued to your side.
Using your bodyweight to push down: stand tall and let the triceps do it.
Letting the handle fly up: control the return.
arm_safety: A short split stance close to the stack is stable; sit on a bench if you feel at all unsteady. To finish, let the handle rise slowly until the stack rests before letting go. Injured arm across your stomach, hand relaxed and away from the cable (or in its sling if you still wear one). Moderate effort (RIR 2–3) and no breath-holding. Physio instructions take priority. Stop if your injured arm aches, throbs, swells, tingles or goes numb, or you notice any red-flag symptom.

name: Seated single-arm dumbbell shoulder press (good arm)
why: Strong, healthy shoulders matter for swinging a pack onto your back, reaching overhead and, later, carrying. Pressing one side while seated also trains your trunk to stay upright against an uneven load.
setup: Only once your clinic or physio has cleared you to train your uninjured arm.
Set the bench upright (80–90°). Take a light dumbbell from the rack with your uninjured hand and sit down with it resting on your thigh.
Lift it to shoulder height with your uninjured arm; a small knee lift can help.
Back against the pad, feet wide and flat; injured arm resting on its own thigh.
cues: Ribs down, back against the pad
Press up and slightly in until the arm is straight overhead
Lower over 2–3 s to just above shoulder height
Don't lean away from the dumbbell
Breathe out as you press
mistakes: Arching your lower back: ribs down, lighter weight.
Bending sideways away from the working arm: stay stacked and use less load.
Elbow flared straight out to the side: keep it slightly in front of your body.
arm_safety: Pick up and put down the dumbbell with your uninjured hand only: at the end, lower it to your shoulder, then your thigh, then return it to the rack or lower it to the floor on your uninjured side. If a rep fails, lower it out to your uninjured side, never towards your injured arm. Injured arm resting on its own thigh, hand relaxed (or in its sling if you still wear one). Moderate effort (RIR 2–3) and no breath-holding. Physio instructions take priority. Stop if your injured arm aches, throbs, swells, tingles or goes numb, or you notice any red-flag symptom.

name: Seated wrist curl (good arm)
why: Forearm strength underpins farmer strength, because every carry starts with the grip. Training your uninjured forearm builds that base now, and in a small trial after wrist fractures, training the uninjured wrist was linked with stronger wrist muscles on the injured side once the cast came off.
setup: Only once your clinic or physio has cleared you to train your uninjured arm.
Sit on a bench and rest your uninjured forearm on your thigh (or along the bench), palm up, wrist just past the knee.
Hold a light dumbbell. Injured arm resting on its own thigh.
Optional: add palm-down (reverse) wrist curls for the extensors.
cues: Forearm stays still on your thigh
Let the wrist bend back slowly; the fingers can uncurl slightly
Curl the wrist up as high as you can and squeeze 1 s
Slow and controlled: 2 s up, 2 s down
mistakes: Lifting the forearm off your thigh: keep it pinned and use a lighter weight.
Bouncing: slow reps through the full range.
Going too heavy: pick a weight you can move smoothly for 12–20 reps.
arm_safety: Seated and stable. Pick up and put down the dumbbell with your uninjured hand only. Injured arm resting on its own thigh, hand open and relaxed (or in its sling if you still wear one); don't let it copy the movement unless your physio has prescribed that. Moderate effort and no breath-holding. Physio instructions take priority. Stop if your injured arm aches, throbs, swells, tingles or goes numb, or you notice any red-flag symptom.

name: Grip squeeze (good hand)
equipment: hand gripper (about £5–10) or a tightly rolled towel
or a dumbbell for timed holds
why: Grip is the limiting factor in farmer-style carries. Squeezing work builds crushing grip in your uninjured hand now, and in a trial after wrist fractures, training the uninjured hand was linked with better grip strength in the injured hand at 12 weeks.
setup: Only once your clinic or physio has cleared you to train your uninjured arm.
Sit on a bench with your uninjured forearm resting on your thigh.
Hold a gripper, stress ball or tightly rolled towel in your uninjured hand. In the gym, a timed hold of a dumbbell hanging at your side while seated works too.
Injured arm resting on its own thigh.
cues: Squeeze hard for 3–5 s, then relax fully
Wrist straight, thumb wrapped round
Breathe out as you squeeze; no breath-holding
For holds: shoulder down, sit tall, hold for time
mistakes: Holding your breath while squeezing: breathe out slowly through each squeeze.
Bending the wrist: keep it straight and strong.
Partial squeezes: close the hand fully (or as far as the gripper allows) and hold.
arm_safety: Seated and stable. Keep your injured hand open and relaxed on its thigh (or the arm in its sling if you still wear one); you may notice it wants to squeeze too, so let it rest. If your physio has prescribed hand exercises for your injured side, do those separately, as prescribed. Physio instructions take priority. Stop if your injured arm aches, throbs, swells, tingles or goes numb, or you notice any red-flag symptom.
dose: 3 × 8–12 hard 3-s squeezes, RIR 2–3

name: Suitcase carry (good hand)
equipment: dumbbell (or kettlebell if your gym has them)
why: A one-sided carry makes your core keep you upright and walking straight, and it builds grip. It isn't in your plan: training carries wait for grip clearance, and with your uninjured hand holding the weight nothing is free to break a stumble. After grip clearance, do it only if your physio suggests a one-handed carry with your uninjured hand while your injured hand builds up.
setup: Only after grip clearance (training carries wait for it), and only if your physio suggests carrying with your uninjured hand alone.
Choose a clear, flat 15–20 m lane with nothing to trip over.
Take the dumbbell from a rack at hip height with your uninjured hand (or pick it up from the floor with a flat back, bending your knees).
Stand tall; injured arm resting across your stomach.
cues: Stand tall; don't lean towards or away from the weight
Shoulders level; pull the carrying shoulder down and back
Brace lightly and keep breathing
Normal, steady steps; eyes ahead
Squeeze the handle hard
mistakes: Leaning away from the weight to balance it: lighter dumbbell, stand tall.
Shrugging the carrying shoulder: pull it down towards your back pocket.
Rushing: walk at a normal pace, because speed hides poor posture.
arm_safety: Normally your uninjured hand is your fall protection, and here it's holding the weight, so if you stumble, drop the dumbbell to the side straight away and keep your injured arm tucked in. Flat, clear, dry floor only; turn slowly at the end of each length. Put the dumbbell down by squatting with a flat back. Once your injured hand reaches the 70% rung (measured by your physio or with their OK), the both-sides suitcase carry replaces this one. Moderate load and no breath-holding. Physio instructions take priority. Stop if your injured arm aches, throbs, swells, tingles or goes numb, you notice any red-flag symptom, or you feel unsteady. Any fall onto the arm: stop and get it checked.
dose: 3–4 × 20–30 m; start light (around 8–12 kg) and add 2 kg when you can walk tall with no lean

name: Finger tendon glides (injured hand)
equipment: table or pillow to support the forearm
why: Typical purpose: keeps the finger tendons sliding freely through the wrist and forearm and helps with finger stiffness, which is the starting point for getting your grip, and so your farmer strength, back. Only as prescribed by your physio; doses here are placeholders.
setup: Use only the version your physio has shown you.
Sit at a table with your forearm supported, elbow bent, wrist relaxed and roughly straight.

Move slowly through five positions: straight hand; hook fist (bend the middle and end finger joints, knuckles straight); full fist; tabletop (bend at the knuckles only, fingers straight); straight fist (bend the knuckles and middle joints, fingertips straight, touching the base of your palm).
Return to the straight hand between positions if your physio prefers.
cues: Slow and gentle; hold each position 3–5 s
Move only as far as is comfortable
Keep the wrist relaxed and still
Breathe normally
mistakes: Forcing the fist with the other hand: active movement only, unless your physio has shown you otherwise.
Rushing through the positions: each one moves the tendons differently, so take your time.
Pushing into sharp pain: back off to a comfortable range.
arm_safety: Do this only if your physio or clinic has prescribed it, and only the way they showed you. Sit with the forearm fully supported. Your physio will tell you how much discomfort is acceptable. Stop and contact your physio or fracture clinic (or NHS 111 out of hours) if pain is sharp or keeps increasing, the hand or forearm swells more, goes numb, tingly, pale, blue or cold, the wound or scar looks red, hot or weeps, or you feel feverish or unwell.
dose: Only as prescribed by your physio; doses here are placeholders. Typical starting point: 5–10 slow rounds, several times a day.

name: Wrist bend up and down (active range of motion)
why: Typical purpose: restores the up-and-down bend of the wrist (flexion and extension), which you'll need for everything from getting up off the floor to carrying and using walking poles. Only as prescribed by your physio; doses here are placeholders.
setup: Use only the version your physio has shown you.
Sit at a table and rest your forearm on a folded towel, hand over the edge, palm down.
Let your fingers relax, or make a loose fist if your physio prefers.
cues: Slowly lift the back of your hand up as far as is comfortable
Then slowly lower it down as far as is comfortable
Forearm stays flat on the towel
Smooth movement with a brief pause at each end
Repeat palm up only if your physio prescribes it
mistakes: Lifting the forearm to cheat the range: keep it pinned to the towel.
Forcing the end of the range with the other hand: only if your physio has taught you assisted stretches.
Fast, jerky reps: slow and smooth.
arm_safety: Do this only if your physio or clinic has prescribed it, and only the way they showed you. Keep the forearm supported throughout. Your physio will tell you how much discomfort is acceptable. Stop and contact your physio or fracture clinic (or NHS 111 out of hours) if pain is sharp or keeps increasing, the hand or forearm swells more, goes numb, tingly, pale, blue or cold, the wound or scar looks red, hot or weeps, or you feel feverish or unwell.
dose: Only as prescribed by your physio; doses here are placeholders. Typical starting point: 10 slow reps, 3–4 times a day.

name: Forearm rotation (palm up, palm down)
equipment: table or thigh to support the forearm
why: Typical purpose: restores turning the palm up (supination) and down (pronation). This movement depends on both forearm bones, so it's a common focus of rehab after forearm fractures, and you need it for door handles, keys, mugs and walking poles. Only as prescribed by your physio; doses here are placeholders.
setup: Use only the version your physio has shown you.
Sit with your elbow bent to 90° and tucked into your side; a rolled towel between elbow and ribs helps.
Forearm supported on a table or your thigh, thumb pointing up.
cues: Slowly turn your palm up to face the ceiling
Then slowly turn it down to face the floor
Elbow stays tucked in; don't let the shoulder do the work
Pause briefly at each end of the comfortable range
mistakes: Elbow drifting away from your body: keep the towel squeezed against your side.
Rotating from the shoulder to fake the range: keep the upper arm still.
Pushing into sharp pain: stay in the comfortable range.
arm_safety: Do this only if your physio or clinic has prescribed it, and only the way they showed you. Keep the forearm supported and the movement slow. Your physio will tell you how much discomfort is acceptable. Stop and contact your physio or fracture clinic (or NHS 111 out of hours) if pain is sharp or keeps increasing, the hand or forearm swells more, goes numb, tingly, pale, blue or cold, the wound or scar looks red, hot or weeps, or you feel feverish or unwell.
dose: Only as prescribed by your physio; doses here are placeholders. Typical starting point: 10 slow reps each way, 3–4 times a day.

name: Wrist side to side (radial and ulnar deviation)
muscles: wrist flexors and extensors (thumb side and little-finger side)
why: Typical purpose: restores the side-to-side movement of the wrist, which you use when pouring, hammering, gripping a walking pole and carrying a bag by its handle. Only as prescribed by your physio; doses here are placeholders.
setup: Use only the version your physio has shown you.
Sit with your forearm resting on a table, palm down and hand flat (or thumb up with the hand over the edge, if that's what your physio shows you).
Keep the forearm still.
cues: Slide your hand towards the thumb side, then towards the little-finger side
Keep the movement at the wrist, not the elbow
Slow and smooth, with a brief pause at each end
Only as far as is comfortable
mistakes: Moving the forearm instead of the wrist: anchor the forearm on the table.
Bending the wrist up or down at the same time: keep the hand flat on the table.
Rushing: slow reps.
arm_safety: Do this only if your physio or clinic has prescribed it, and only the way they showed you. Keep the forearm supported. Your physio will tell you how much discomfort is acceptable. Stop and contact your physio or fracture clinic (or NHS 111 out of hours) if pain is sharp or keeps increasing, the hand or forearm swells more, goes numb, tingly, pale, blue or cold, the wound or scar looks red, hot or weeps, or you feel feverish or unwell.
dose: Only as prescribed by your physio; doses here are placeholders. Typical starting point: 10 slow reps each way, 3–4 times a day.

name: Elbow bend and straighten (active range of motion)
why: Typical purpose: keeps or restores full elbow bending and straightening, which can stiffen after a forearm fracture and a period of protecting the arm. A straight elbow matters for carrying, and a full bend for eating and washing. Only as prescribed by your physio; doses here are placeholders.
setup: Use only the version your physio has shown you.
Sit or stand tall with your upper arm by your side, or supported on a table if your physio prefers.
Start with the palm facing up; your physio may also ask for palm-down or thumb-up versions.
cues: Slowly bend the elbow, bringing your hand towards your shoulder
Then slowly straighten it as far as is comfortable
Shoulder relaxed and still
Pause briefly at each end
mistakes: Swinging the arm: slow, controlled movement.
Shrugging the shoulder: keep it down and relaxed.
Forcing the last few degrees: stay gentle; consistency beats force.
arm_safety: Do this only if your physio or clinic has prescribed it, and only the way they showed you. Move slowly and don't swing the arm. Your physio will tell you how much discomfort is acceptable. Stop and contact your physio or fracture clinic (or NHS 111 out of hours) if pain is sharp or keeps increasing, the hand or forearm swells more, goes numb, tingly, pale, blue or cold, the wound or scar looks red, hot or weeps, or you feel feverish or unwell.
dose: Only as prescribed by your physio; doses here are placeholders. Typical starting point: 10 slow reps, 3–4 times a day.

name: Therapy putty grip work
equipment: therapy putty (grade chosen by your physio)
why: Typical purpose: an early step in rebuilding grip strength, with resistance that can be fine-tuned. Grip is the base of your farmer-strength goal, so this is where that journey restarts for your injured hand. Only as prescribed by your physio; doses here are placeholders.
setup: Use only the version your physio has shown you.
Sit at a table with your forearm supported.
Use the putty grade your physio gives you, usually the softest to begin with.
Common drills: full-hand squeeze; pinching between the thumb and each fingertip; spreading the fingers against a putty ring.
cues: Squeeze slowly and steadily, then relax fully
Re-form the putty into a ball between sets
Wrist straight and relaxed
Quality over quantity
mistakes: Using putty that's too firm: start soft and progress only when your physio says so.
Squeezing hard and fast to exhaustion: slow, controlled squeezes.
Wrist bending as you squeeze: keep it in line with your forearm.
arm_safety: Do this only if your physio or clinic has prescribed it, and only the way they showed you. Never move up a putty grade on your own. Your physio will tell you how much discomfort is acceptable. Stop and contact your physio or fracture clinic (or NHS 111 out of hours) if pain is sharp or keeps increasing, the hand or forearm swells more, goes numb, tingly, pale, blue or cold, the wound or scar looks red, hot or weeps, or you feel feverish or unwell.
dose: Only as prescribed by your physio; doses here are placeholders. Typical starting point: 2–3 sets of 10 squeezes, once or twice a day.

name: Towel wringing
equipment: small hand towel (dry unless your physio says otherwise)
why: Typical purpose: combines grip with forearm rotation in both directions, a practical step towards wringing cloths, opening jars and handling ropes and handles. Only as prescribed by your physio; doses here are placeholders.
setup: Use only the version your physio has shown you.
Sit at a table and roll a small towel into a tube.
Hold it with both hands in front of you, elbows bent and close to your sides.
cues: Twist gently in one direction, as if wringing water out
Then twist the other way
Light effort to start; this isn't a strength test
Elbows stay by your sides
mistakes: Wringing hard straight away: start gently; your physio sets the effort.
Twisting with your shoulders: keep the movement in the forearms and wrists.
Using a big, wet towel too soon: small, dry towel first.
arm_safety: Do this only if your physio or clinic has prescribed it, and only the way they showed you. Let your injured side set the effort; your uninjured hand must not overpower it. Your physio will tell you how much discomfort is acceptable. Stop and contact your physio or fracture clinic (or NHS 111 out of hours) if pain is sharp or keeps increasing, the hand or forearm swells more, goes numb, tingly, pale, blue or cold, the wound or scar looks red, hot or weeps, or you feel feverish or unwell.
dose: Only as prescribed by your physio; doses here are placeholders. Typical starting point: 5–10 slow twists each way.

name: Light wrist curl (injured side)
equipment: very light dumbbell or a tin of food (as prescribed)
why: Typical purpose: begins gently loading the forearm flexors once movement has returned, rebuilding the strength you need for holding and carrying. Only as prescribed by your physio; doses here are placeholders.
setup: Use only the version your physio has shown you.
Sit with your forearm supported on a folded towel on a table or your thigh, palm up, hand over the edge.
Hold the weight your physio has prescribed; often something like 0.5–1 kg or a tin of beans to begin with.
cues: Let the wrist lower slowly
Curl the wrist up as far as is comfortable and pause 1 s
Forearm stays flat on the support
Slow: 2–3 s each way
mistakes: Increasing the weight on your own: your physio decides when.
Lifting the forearm off the support: keep it anchored.
Letting the weight drop quickly: control the lowering.
arm_safety: Do this only if your physio or clinic has prescribed it, and only the way they showed you. Pick the weight up and put it down with your uninjured hand, and never add weight on your own. Your physio will tell you how much discomfort is acceptable. Stop and contact your physio or fracture clinic (or NHS 111 out of hours) if pain is sharp or keeps increasing, the hand or forearm swells more, goes numb, tingly, pale, blue or cold, the wound or scar looks red, hot or weeps, or you feel feverish or unwell.
dose: Only as prescribed by your physio; doses here are placeholders. Typical starting point: 2–3 × 10–15 with a very light weight.

name: Light reverse wrist curl (injured side)
equipment: very light dumbbell or a tin of food (as prescribed)
why: Typical purpose: strengthens the wrist extensors, which hold the wrist steady whenever you grip; a strong grip needs strong extensors as well as flexors. Only as prescribed by your physio; doses here are placeholders.
setup: Use only the version your physio has shown you.
Sit with your forearm supported on a folded towel on a table or your thigh, palm down, hand over the edge.
Hold the weight your physio has prescribed, usually lighter than for the palm-up curl.
cues: Let the hand lower slowly
Lift the back of the hand up as far as is comfortable and pause 1 s
Forearm stays flat on the support
Slow: 2–3 s each way
mistakes: Increasing the weight on your own: your physio decides when.
Lifting the forearm or elbow to help: keep it anchored.
Letting the weight drop quickly: control the lowering.
arm_safety: Do this only if your physio or clinic has prescribed it, and only the way they showed you. Pick the weight up and put it down with your uninjured hand, and never add weight on your own. Your physio will tell you how much discomfort is acceptable. Stop and contact your physio or fracture clinic (or NHS 111 out of hours) if pain is sharp or keeps increasing, the hand or forearm swells more, goes numb, tingly, pale, blue or cold, the wound or scar looks red, hot or weeps, or you feel feverish or unwell.
dose: Only as prescribed by your physio; doses here are placeholders. Typical starting point: 2–3 × 10–15 with a very light weight.

name: Hammer rotation (light)
equipment: light hammer, or a light dumbbell held at one end
table or thigh to support the forearm
why: Typical purpose: adds gentle load to forearm rotation using leverage (hold near the head to make it easier, further down the handle to make it harder). It rebuilds the turning strength you need for twisting, turning and handling tools. Only as prescribed by your physio; doses here are placeholders.
setup: Use only the version your physio has shown you.
Sit with your elbow bent to 90° and tucked into your side, forearm supported on a table or your thigh.
Hold the hammer handle with the head pointing up, gripping close to the head to begin.
cues: Slowly rotate so the head tips towards the palm-up side, then back to upright
Then towards the palm-down side, then back to upright
Elbow stays tucked and the forearm still
Slow and controlled; never let it flop
mistakes: Holding too far down the handle too soon: grip closer to the head to reduce the load.
Letting the hammer drop to the end of the range: control it the whole way.
Elbow drifting from your side: tuck a rolled towel under the arm.
arm_safety: Do this only if your physio or clinic has prescribed it, and only the way they showed you. Keep the lever short until your physio says otherwise. Your physio will tell you how much discomfort is acceptable. Stop and contact your physio or fracture clinic (or NHS 111 out of hours) if pain is sharp or keeps increasing, the hand or forearm swells more, goes numb, tingly, pale, blue or cold, the wound or scar looks red, hot or weeps, or you feel feverish or unwell.
dose: Only as prescribed by your physio; doses here are placeholders. Typical starting point: 2–3 × 10 each way.

name: Rice bucket hand work
equipment: bucket or deep bowl of dry rice
why: Typical purpose: the rice gives gentle resistance in every direction, training gripping, finger opening and wrist and forearm movement all at once. It's a classic grip drill and a useful bridge towards the grip strength your carries need. Only as prescribed by your physio; doses here are placeholders.
setup: Use only the version your physio has shown you, and only once your wound and scar are fully healed.
Fill a bucket or deep bowl with dry rice and place it on a table at a comfortable height.
Sit beside it so you can push your hand in without straining your shoulder.
cues: Push the hand in gently, only as deep as is comfortable
Open and close the hand; spread the fingers
Turn the palm up and down; move the wrist side to side
Move slowly and stop well before fatigue
mistakes: Plunging in deep and hard: start shallow and gentle.
Going on for many minutes: keep sessions as short as your physio prescribes.
Ignoring your skin: check with your physio that the scar is ready, and stop if it gets sore or irritated.
arm_safety: Do this only if your physio or clinic has prescribed it, the way they showed you, and only on fully healed skin. Your physio will tell you how much discomfort is acceptable. Stop and contact your physio or fracture clinic (or NHS 111 out of hours) if pain is sharp or keeps increasing, the hand or forearm swells more, goes numb, tingly, pale, blue or cold, the wound or scar looks red, hot or weeps, or you feel feverish or unwell.
dose: Only as prescribed by your physio; doses here are placeholders. Typical starting point: 1–3 minutes of mixed movements.

name: Light ruck (walking with a light rucksack)
equipment: rucksack with hip belt and sternum strap
light load (water bottles, a bag of rice, or a small plate wrapped in a towel)
why: Long-distance hiking means carrying a pack for hours. Starting very light lets your feet, legs, back and shoulders adapt gradually, so that proper hiking loads feel normal later.
setup: Only once your clinic has cleared you for light use of your injured arm.
Start with 2–4 kg, and keep it light (no more than about 10% of your bodyweight) until full clearance.
Pack the weight high and close to your back, and pad any hard objects.
Fit: hip belt on top of your hip bones carrying most of the load, shoulder straps snug, sternum strap clipped.
Route: incline treadmill or good, even paths, with the same terrain rules as your hikes.
cues: Tall posture with a very slight lean from the ankles
Short, steady steps, especially downhill
Your hips carry the load, not your shoulders
Stay in Zone 2: you can talk but would rather not
Add about 1 kg every 2–3 weeks, only if the walk and the next morning felt fine
mistakes: Adding weight and distance in the same week: change one thing at a time.
Loose hip belt, so the load hangs off your shoulders: tighten it on your hip bones.
Hunching forward: lighten the pack and stand tall.
arm_safety: Putting it on, seated: sit on a bench with the pack beside you, slide your uninjured arm through its strap and lift the pack onto your back with that arm, then ease your injured arm into the other strap without gripping or pushing; fasten the hip belt and sternum strap with your uninjured hand, then stand. Taking it off: sit down, unclip with your uninjured hand, slide the strap off your injured side first, then lower the pack with your uninjured arm. Never swing it on or off. Check that no strap rubs or presses on a scar or the fracture site. A pack makes a stumble harder to recover from, so the terrain rules are strict: even surfaces, no ice, mud or loose ground, and extra care on descents. Stop if arm pain rises, it throbs, swells, tingles or goes numb, or you notice any red-flag symptom. Any fall onto the arm: stop and get it checked.
dose: Your Saturday long walk: 80 min in Zone 2 with 2–4 kg to start, adding about 1 kg every 2–3 weeks if the walk and next morning feel fine; keep it to about 10% of your body weight (8 kg for the 80 kg example profile) until full clearance

name: Your physio's programme
why: Your physiotherapist's prescription is the only rehab you do on your injured arm. This slot reserves daily time for it, so it happens every day and gets logged.
setup: Have your physio's written exercise sheet to hand (add the exercises on the Your arm page; the daily rehab slot appears once they are entered).
Sit at a table in a quiet spot, warm and relaxed.
cues: Do exactly the exercises, doses and pain limits your physio gave you, nothing extra.
Move slowly and smoothly through the range they want.
Note pain before and after on the Your arm page.
mistakes: Adding exercises from the internet or this library that weren't prescribed. Stick to the sheet.
Pushing into pain to 'speed things up'. Stay within the limit your physio set (if you weren't given one, 2/10 or less, settled by the next morning).
arm_safety: Only what your physio has prescribed. The rehab-* entries in this library are background reading, not a prescription. Stop and contact your fracture clinic for any red flag: increasing pain, new swelling, redness or heat, discharge, fever, numbness or colour change.
dose: As prescribed by your physio (about 10–15 min, usually daily)

name: Goblet squat
equipment: dumbbell (or a kettlebell if your gym has them)
bench or box as a depth target
why: Your first loaded squat once you can hold a weight. Holding the weight in front teaches an upright torso and a braced trunk, which is the posture you need on steps and stiles with a pack. It also builds the quads and glutes that will carry most of your first kilos of new muscle.
setup: Stand a dumbbell on its end on a bench. Cup the top plate with both palms, thumbs around the handle, and lift it to your breastbone with your elbows pointing down. (With a kettlebell, hold it by the horns.)
Feet a little wider than hip-width, toes turned out 10–30°, weight over the middle of each foot.
Put a bench or box behind you at a height you can sit to with control. Lower it over the weeks.
Breathe in through your nose into your belly and sides, then brace moderately.
cues: Sit down between your heels.
Knees travel out over your little toes.
Dumbbell glued to your breastbone, chest proud.
Spread the floor with your feet.
Exhale as you stand, and finish tall with your glutes squeezed.
mistakes: Dumbbell drifting away from the chest, which strains the forearms and tips you forward. Fix: keep it touching your breastbone. If you can't, it's too heavy.
Knees caving in. Fix: push them out over your little toes, slow the lowering and go lighter.
Heels lifting. Fix: widen your stance a little, turn your toes out more, squat to a higher box and keep doing ankle-knee-to-wall.
Dropping onto the box and rocking up. Fix: take three seconds down, touch lightly, then stand without rocking.
arm_safety: Only after your physio has cleared gripping and holding weights. The goblet hold spreads the load across both palms with your wrists close to neutral, so it's the gentlest way to start loading your injured arm in a squat. Use 6–10 kg for the first two weeks, even if your legs could take far more, and let the leg press keep doing the heavy leg work. If your forearm or wrist tires before your legs do, you've found your limit for now. Pick the dumbbell up from a bench and put it back there, so you never lift it off the floor. Arm rule: stay within your physio's pain limit (if you haven't been given one, 2/10 or less during the set), settled by the next morning, no new swelling. Otherwise go back to box-squat-bw. Fall risk is low. Squat to a box, and if you lose balance, sit on it rather than putting a hand down.
dose: Phase 2: 3 × 8, RIR 3, tempo 3-1-1-0, a light counterweight (6–10 kg). Later 3 × 8–12, RIR 2–3; add 2 kg when every set reaches 12.

name: Smith machine squat
equipment: bench or box as a depth target (optional)
why: The Smith machine's fixed bar path and built-in catches let you load the squat beyond what a goblet hold allows. Your hands only steady the bar. It's the bridge to the free-bar back squat and more leg muscle for long ascents.
setup: Do a bodyweight squat under the bar first, then set the safety stops just below the bar's lowest point.
Set the bar at upper-chest height, step under it and rest it on the muscle of your upper back, not your neck.
Grip a little wider than your shoulders with your wrists straight. Your hands steady the bar; they don't hold the weight.
Put your feet 10–20 cm in front of the bar line, hip- to shoulder-width apart, toes slightly out.
Breathe in, brace moderately, then twist the bar off its hooks.
cues: Sit down and slightly back; knees follow your toes.
Whole foot planted. Push the floor away.
Chest up, upper back tight against the bar.
Exhale as you drive up, then breathe again at the top.
At the end of the set, twist the bar onto the nearest hook.
mistakes: Feet directly under the bar, so your knees shoot forward and your heels lift. Fix: move your feet forward until you can sit down with the whole foot pressing.
Forgetting the safety stops. Fix: set them before your first set, every time. They're your spotter.
Wrists bent back under the bar. Fix: change your grip width until both wrists stay straight. The bar sits on your back, not in your hands.
Bouncing out of the bottom. Fix: three seconds down, then drive up.
arm_safety: Start only once your physio has cleared gripping and holding weights and you can hold an empty bar comfortably with both hands. Hooking and unhooking a Smith bar means twisting it with your wrists, so practise that with no plates first. Use the bar alone for the first one or two weeks, then add no more than 2.5 kg a side per session. Smith bars range from counterbalanced and very light to about 20 kg, so ask staff what yours weighs. Load the plates evenly; your uninjured hand carries plates of 10 kg or less, and staff help with heavier ones. If your injured wrist or elbow aches while holding the bar in place, go back to goblet squats. Arm rule: stay within your physio's pain limit (if you haven't been given one, 2/10 or less during the set), settled by the next morning, no new swelling. Fall risk is low. The bar only moves up and down and the stops catch it, so if a rep fails, sit down under it and let it land on the stops.
dose: 3–4 × 5–8, RIR 2, tempo 3-1-1-0. Empty bar first. Add 2.5–5 kg in total when every set reaches the top of the range.

name: Barbell back squat
why: A classic whole-body strength builder. Once your arm can share the job, the back squat lets you add load to your legs and trunk for years. That means more muscle for your 5 kg goal and strong legs for long climbs and descents with a pack.
setup: Set the bar on the rack hooks at mid-chest height, low enough that you bend your knees slightly to get under it.
Set the safety arms 3–5 cm below where the bar sits at the bottom of your squat. Check it with the empty bar.
Take a grip a little wider than your shoulders, thumbs around the bar and wrists straight. Duck under and place the bar on your upper traps, above your shoulder blades (high-bar).
Squeeze your shoulder blades together to make a shelf. Stand the bar up and take two or three small steps back, no more.
Feet about shoulder-width, toes out 15–30°. Breathe in and brace moderately.
cues: Break at the hips and knees together and sit down between your heels.
Knees out over your toes, whole foot planted.
Bar over the middle of your foot the whole way.
Chest and bar rise together. Don't let your hips shoot up first.
Exhale through pursed lips past the hardest part, then breathe and brace again at the top.
mistakes: Hips rising faster than the chest (a 'good-morning' squat). Fix: go lighter, think 'chest up, push the floor away' and pause 1 s at the bottom.
Walking the bar out too far. Fix: two or three small steps, so the hooks are right there when you re-rack.
Bar rolling up your neck or down your back. Fix: squeeze your shoulder blades, keep your elbows under the bar and hold it only as tightly as your injured hand finds comfortable.
No safeties set. Fix: never squat without the safety arms. With them set, you can sit down and leave a failed rep on the arms.
arm_safety: Full clearance only: your plan brings it in at Phase 4a, after months of Smith squats. Ask your physio specifically about holding a bar on your back, because the position turns your shoulders out and can bend your wrists back. Use the empty 20 kg bar for the first sessions, then add no more than 2.5 kg a side per session. Pick a grip width (usually wider) where both wrists stay straight and the bar sits on your back, not in your hands. Use moderate bracing and keep breathing while you learn it; heavy sets of 1–5 with a brief full brace come later, once the lift is grooved. Arm rule: stay within your physio's pain limit (if you haven't been given one, 2/10 or less during the set), settled by the next morning, no new swelling. Fall risk is medium, because a failed rep or a stumble on the walk-out can make you reach out. Always squat inside the rack with the safety arms set just below your lowest point. A failed rep then goes onto the arms and you never have to dump the bar.
dose: 3–4 × 4–6, RIR 2–3, tempo 2-1-1-0. Empty bar first. Add 2.5–5 kg in total while every rep looks the same on video.

name: Dumbbell split squat
equipment: squat rack upright or wall to touch
why: Trains each leg on its own, which shows up left–right differences and builds the hip stability you need on uneven trails. Holding a dumbbell adds load and makes your trunk resist leaning.
setup: Stand side-on to a rack upright with your uninjured hand on it.
Take a long split stance with your feet hip-width apart, like on train tracks rather than a tightrope. Front foot flat, back foot on the ball.
Until full clearance, hold one dumbbell in your injured hand, arm long, shoulder down. Your uninjured hand stays on the rack.
After full clearance, hold a dumbbell in each hand at your sides.
cues: Drop the back knee straight down towards the floor.
Front foot does the work, with the whole foot pressing.
Stay tall, shoulders over hips, and don't lean towards the weight.
Drive up through the front foot and exhale.
Finish all the reps on one leg, then switch.
mistakes: Stance too narrow, so you wobble. Fix: widen your feet side to side.
Pushing off the back foot. Fix: the back leg is a kickstand; the front leg works.
Leaning towards the dumbbell side. Fix: go lighter and stay tall.
Back knee banging the floor. Fix: stop 2–3 cm above it, or put a folded mat under it.
arm_safety: After grip clearance. Until full clearance, the safety rule is that balance work happens next to a support your uninjured hand can touch. So hold one dumbbell in your injured hand and keep your uninjured hand on the rack. The weight is whatever your injured hand can hold comfortably for the whole set, usually 4–8 kg to start. Your legs still get equal work. After full clearance, progress to a dumbbell in each hand, equal weights. Arm rule: stay within your physio's pain limit (if you haven't been given one, 2/10 or less during the set), settled by the next morning, no new swelling. Fall risk is medium. If you wobble, hold the rack, stand up out of the split and bring your feet together. Put the dumbbell down rather than reaching out with your injured arm.
dose: 3 × 8–10 / side, RIR 2–3, tempo 2-0-1-0. Add 2 kg when every set reaches 10 with control.

name: Dumbbell Bulgarian split squat
equipment: rack upright next to the bench
why: One of the best leg builders for a hiker. It works the knee and hip deeply on one leg and stretches the glutes hard, with little load on your spine. In one training study, it matched the back squat for strength gains.
setup: Put a flat bench next to a rack upright. Stand facing away from the bench with your uninjured hand towards the rack.
Rest the top of your back foot (laces down) on the bench.
Hop your front foot forward until your front shin is roughly vertical at the bottom, usually 60–90 cm from the bench.
Until full clearance, hold one dumbbell in your injured hand with your uninjured hand on the rack. After full clearance, hold one in each hand.
Square your hips, breathe in and brace moderately.
cues: Sink straight down; the front leg does nearly all the work.
A slight forward lean works the glutes more; staying taller works the quads more.
Front knee follows your second toe.
Exhale and push the floor away through your whole front foot.
mistakes: Front foot too close, so your heel lifts. Fix: move it further forward.
Bouncing off the back foot. Fix: the bench holds your back leg; it isn't a springboard.
Bench too high, so the back hip strains and balance suffers. Fix: use a lower surface or go back to db-split-squat.
Hips twisting. Fix: keep both hip bones facing forward and slow the lowering.
arm_safety: After grip clearance, and only once bodyweight rear-foot-elevated split squats are steady. This has the highest balance demand of the Part B leg exercises. Until full clearance, use one light dumbbell in your injured hand and keep your uninjured hand on a rack upright next to the bench. After full clearance, use a dumbbell in each hand, equal weights. Arm rule: stay within your physio's pain limit (if you haven't been given one, 2/10 or less during the set), settled by the next morning, no new swelling. Fall risk is medium. Get in and out of position slowly, and put the dumbbell down before you take your foot off the bench. If you lose balance, step your back foot down to the floor.
dose: 3 × 8–10 / side, RIR 2, tempo 3-0-1-0. Add 2 kg when every set reaches 10.

name: Dumbbell step-up
equipment: until full clearance: an aerobic step (15–25 cm) or the bottom stair; after it, a stable box or flat bench up to knee height
why: The most hiking-specific strength exercise there is. Stepping up under load is what every climb, stile and rock step asks of you, and adding weight builds the single-leg strength to do it for hours with a rucksack.
setup: Until full clearance: an aerobic step (15–25 cm) beside the rack, never a bench. After full clearance: a stable box or flat bench up to knee height, starting at 30–40 cm. Check it doesn't wobble or slide.
Place it beside a rack upright, on your uninjured side.
Until full clearance, hold one dumbbell in your injured hand, or wear your day pack (hands free), and keep your uninjured hand near or on the rack. After full clearance, hold one in each hand.
Put your whole foot on the box.
cues: Lean slightly forward and push through the top foot. Don't spring off the bottom leg.
Stand fully tall at the top, hips under shoulders.
Lower slowly, over 3 s. This is your downhill training.
Exhale on the way up.
mistakes: Pushing off the bottom foot. Fix: keep the back foot's toes light and pause briefly on the floor between reps.
Knee caving in on the way up. Fix: keep it over your second toe and go lighter.
Dropping down fast. Fix: control the lowering, because downhill knees need it.
Box so high that your hip hikes. Fix: lower it until you can step up without twisting.
arm_safety: After grip clearance, and only once bodyweight step-ups to the same height are steady. Until full clearance, hold one dumbbell in your injured hand with your uninjured hand on or near the rack. After full clearance, hold a dumbbell in each hand. Start light (4–8 kg) on the aerobic step; higher boxes and benches wait for full clearance. Arm rule: stay within your physio's pain limit (if you haven't been given one, 2/10 or less during the set), settled by the next morning, no new swelling. Fall risk is medium, mostly from catching a toe on the edge. Look at the box, place your whole foot and step down backwards slowly. Never step onto stacked plates or anything that can slide.
dose: 3 × 8 / side, RIR 2–3, 3 s lowering. Before full clearance, add load (+2 kg) on the aerobic step; after it, raise the height (up to knee level), then the load.

name: Dumbbell walking lunge
equipment: clear, dry, flat lane of 10–20 m
why: Single-leg strength on the move. Every step is a controlled brake and push-off, like walking downhill and over rough ground, so it combines leg strength, balance and grip in one drill.
setup: Clear a straight lane of at least 10 m on a non-slip floor.
Hold light dumbbells at your sides and stand tall.
Step forward one long stride, feet hip-width apart.
cues: Step, sink the back knee towards the floor, then push through the front foot and bring the back leg through.
Tall torso, eyes on the floor 3–4 m ahead.
Front knee tracks your toes, whole foot flat.
One breath per step, breathing out as you rise.
mistakes: Steps too short (heel lifts) or too long (overreaching). Fix: aim for both knees at about 90° at the bottom.
Wobbling side to side. Fix: walk on train tracks, not a tightrope, and slow down.
Rushing when tired. Fix: end the set when your control drops.
arm_safety: Gated at full clearance, one gate later than the default for dumbbell work, because this is the least stable leg exercise in the library. You travel forward on one leg with both hands full and nothing to hold, which doesn't fit the rule that balance work happens next to a support until full clearance. Until then, split squats and step-ups next to a rack do the same job. When you start, do bodyweight walking lunges for a session or two, then 4–6 kg per hand, equal weights. Arm rule: stay within your physio's pain limit (if you haven't been given one, 2/10 or less during the set), settled by the next morning, no new swelling. Fall risk is medium. Use a clean, dry, flat floor only, and never lunge when you're very tired. If you lose balance, step wide and put the dumbbells down rather than reaching out.
dose: 2–3 × 8–10 steps / leg, RIR 2–3. Add 2 kg per hand when every set feels controlled.

name: Dumbbell Romanian deadlift
why: Teaches the hip hinge under load, which is how you should lift a rucksack, a sandbag or anything else off the ground. It builds the hamstrings and glutes that drive you uphill, and dumbbells let you start very light with your wrists in a natural position.
setup: Pick the dumbbells up from a bench or rack at thigh height, not from the floor.
Stand tall, feet hip-width, knees soft, dumbbells in front of your thighs. Palms can face you or each other.
Pull your shoulders down and slightly back, breathe in and brace moderately.
cues: Push your hips back as if closing a car door with your bum.
Dumbbells slide down your thighs, close to your legs.
Shins stay almost vertical; knees stay soft and don't bend further.
Go down until you feel a strong hamstring stretch, usually just below the knees, with a long spine.
Drive your hips forward to stand, squeeze your glutes and exhale.
mistakes: Rounding your back to reach lower. Fix: stop where your back would round. Depth comes as your hamstrings lengthen.
Turning it into a squat. Fix: keep the shins vertical and push the hips back.
Dumbbells drifting forward. Fix: keep them brushing your legs.
Leaning back at the top. Fix: finish tall, ribs down, glutes tight.
arm_safety: After grip clearance. In an RDL your hands hold the full load for the whole set, so your grip will limit the weight before your hamstrings do, and for now that's the right limiter. Start with 4–8 kg per hand, equal weights, palms facing each other if that's kinder to your injured wrist. Don't use lifting straps to get round a weak grip. They let you hold more than your hand can and switch off your grip as the warning light. Take the dumbbells from a bench and put them back there, so there's no floor pick-up. Arm rule: stay within your physio's pain limit (if you haven't been given one, 2/10 or less during the set), settled by the next morning, no new swelling. Fall risk is low.
dose: 3 × 8–10, RIR 2–3, tempo 3-0-1-1 (3 s down, 1 s squeeze at the top). Add 2 kg per hand when every set reaches 10.

name: Barbell Romanian deadlift
equipment: squat rack (to take the bar at thigh height)
why: The barbell lets you load the hinge further than dumbbells, building the posterior chain for climbing, carrying and a resilient back. Taking the bar from the rack means you never pull it from the floor.
setup: Set the bar on the rack hooks at mid-thigh height and set the safety arms just below your lowest RDL position.
Grip just outside your thighs with both palms facing you, thumbs around, wrists straight.
Stand up with the bar, take one or two steps back, feet hip-width.
Shoulders down and back, chest proud. Breathe in and brace moderately.
cues: Hips back; the bar slides down your thighs.
Knees soft, shins vertical.
Bar stays touching your legs, over the middle of your feet.
Stop at the hamstring stretch, usually just below the knee or mid-shin.
Push your hips through, stand tall and exhale.
mistakes: Bar drifting away from your legs. Fix: with straight arms, pull it into you as if bending the bar round your legs.
Upper back rounding at the bottom. Fix: go lighter and stop higher.
Squatting it down. Fix: knees stay soft and the hips go back.
Leaning back at the top. Fix: stand tall, ribs down, and finish with your glutes.
arm_safety: After grip clearance, once dumbbell RDLs feel easy on your grip. A barbell makes both hands share the load, so if your injured hand is weaker the bar will want to tilt. Keep the weight where the bar stays level without effort. Start with the empty bar and add 2.5–5 kg per session at most. Use a double overhand grip with straight wrists, no straps and no mixed (one palm up) grip. Take the bar from the rack hooks at thigh height and return it there, so you never lower it to the floor. Arm rule: stay within your physio's pain limit (if you haven't been given one, 2/10 or less during the set), settled by the next morning, no new swelling. Fall risk is low.
dose: 3 × 6–8, RIR 2, tempo 3-1-1-0. Empty bar first. Add 5 kg when every set reaches 8.

name: Kettlebell deadlift
equipment: kettlebell (no kettlebells? a dumbbell beside each foot, lifted as a 'suitcase deadlift')
why: StrongFirst teaches this before any swing: a light weight lifted from between your feet with a perfect hinge. It's how you'll lift everything in daily life, and it's your gateway to kettlebell swings for conditioning.
setup: Stand with the kettlebell between your feet, handle in line with the middle of your feet, feet a little wider than your hips. (No kettlebell? Stand a dumbbell beside each foot.)
Push your hips back and bend your knees as much as you need to reach the handle with a flat back. Shins stay nearly vertical.
Grip the handle with both hands and pull your shoulders away from your ears.
Breathe into your belly and feel tension in your hamstrings and lats before you lift.
cues: Push the floor away and stand up tall.
Hips and shoulders rise together.
At the top, stand like a plank: glutes and quads tight, ribs down.
On the way down, hips go back first and the bell lands between your feet.
Exhale with a sharp hiss at the top.
mistakes: Squatting down to it, with knees forward and hips low. Fix: push the hips back further. As a drill, stand a foot from a wall and touch it with your bum.
Rounding your back to reach the handle. Fix: raise the bell on a plate or widen your stance.
Yanking with your arms. Fix: arms are straight ropes. Take up the tension first, then push the floor away.
Leaning back at the top. Fix: finish vertical.
arm_safety: After grip clearance. Start with 8–12 kg, light enough that your injured hand is never the struggle, with both hands sharing the handle equally. With dumbbells, use the same weight in each hand. Lower the weight with the same hinge you lifted it with; never drop it. Arm rule: stay within your physio's pain limit (if you haven't been given one, 2/10 or less during the set), settled by the next morning, no new swelling. Fall risk is low. This is your entry ticket to kettlebell swings, which wait for full clearance.
dose: 3 × 5–8, RIR 2–3. Crisp, identical reps, no grinding. Add 4 kg (or 2 kg per dumbbell) when every rep looks the same.

name: Barbell deadlift
equipment: full-size (45 cm) plates, or blocks to raise the bar
why: The king of farmer strength: picking a heavy object up from the floor. Done well and progressed patiently, it builds the back, hips and grip that make carrying, rucking and lifting feel easy.
setup: Use full-size plates so the bar starts at mid-shin height. If you only have small plates, raise the bar on blocks or stacked plates.
Stand with the bar over the middle of your feet, 2–3 cm from your shins, feet hip-width and toes slightly out.
Hinge down and grip just outside your legs, both palms facing you, thumbs around.
Bend your knees until your shins touch the bar. Chest up, back flat, shoulders slightly in front of the bar.
Take the slack out: arms straight, lats tight, as if bending the bar round your legs. Breathe in and brace moderately.
cues: Push the floor away. Don't pull with your back.
Bar stays in contact with your legs the whole way, in a straight vertical line.
Hips and shoulders rise together until the bar passes your knees, then drive your hips forward.
Finish tall with your glutes tight and no leaning back.
Lower it the same way: hips back first, then bend the knees once the bar passes them.
mistakes: Bar too far from your shins at the start. Fix: set it over the middle of your foot.
Hips shooting up first. Fix: take the slack out before the plates leave the floor and keep your chest up.
Jerking the bar off the floor. Fix: slack out, then squeeze it up.
Lower back rounding. Fix: reduce the load, and raise the bar on blocks to shorten the range while your hinge improves.
arm_safety: Full clearance only (your plan brings it in at Phase 4), after many weeks of RDLs that feel easy on your grip. The deadlift asks more of your hands than any other lift, so your injured hand decides the weight. Start with the empty bar set at mid-shin height on blocks, then add 2.5–5 kg a session. Stop adding weight when your injured hand can't comfortably hold every rep with both palms facing you. Use no straps and no mixed grip, which loads one forearm fully palm-up under heavy weight. Use moderate bracing and keep breathing while you learn it; heavy sets of 1–3 with a brief full brace come later. Arm rule: stay within your physio's pain limit (if you haven't been given one, 2/10 or less during the set), settled by the next morning, no new swelling. Fall risk is low.
dose: 3 × 3–5, RIR 2. Set the bar down fully and reset before each rep. Add 5 kg per session while your form holds. No grinders.

name: Barbell hip thrust
equipment: flat bench against a wall or rack
why: It loads the glutes harder than almost any other exercise, with little stress on your back. Strong glutes keep your pelvis stable on every step of a long hike and add size where it counts.
setup: Wedge a bench against a wall or rack so it can't slide. Sit on the floor with your upper back, just below the shoulder blades, against its edge.
Roll a padded bar over your legs to your hip crease. Full-size plates make this easier because the bar rolls instead of needing a lift.
Feet flat and hip-width, 30–40 cm from your bum, so your shins are vertical at the top.
Rest your hands on the bar only to stop it rolling. Tuck your chin.
cues: Chin tucked, eyes forward, ribs down.
Drive through your heels and lift your hips until your body is a tabletop from shoulders to knees.
Squeeze your glutes hard for 1–2 s at the top.
Lower under control and touch lightly. Don't rest at the bottom.
mistakes: Arching your lower back at the top. Fix: keep your ribs down, tuck your pelvis and stop at a flat tabletop.
Feet too far forward, so your hamstrings cramp, or too close, so your quads take over. Fix: move them until your shins are vertical at the top.
Bench sliding. Fix: wedge it against a rack or wall.
Bar rolling towards your belly. Fix: set it in the hip crease on a thick pad and keep your hands on it.
arm_safety: After grip clearance. Rolling the bar into place and steadying it is a two-handed job, so practise with the empty bar or a dumbbell on your hips first. Load plates evenly, and ask staff to help with heavy ones. Your hands only steady the bar; they don't push or hold it. To get up, roll the bar back down your thighs, turn to your uninjured side and stand up using your uninjured hand on the bench. Never push up through your injured wrist before full clearance. Arm rule: stay within your physio's pain limit (if you haven't been given one, 2/10 or less during the set), settled by the next morning, no new swelling. Fall risk is low.
dose: 3 × 8–12, RIR 2, 1–2 s squeeze at the top. Add 5 kg when every set reaches 12.

name: Chest press machine
why: The safest way to start pressing with both arms, with a fixed path, nothing to balance and a load you change with one pin. It rebuilds the upper-body pushing strength you need for scrambling and getting up off the ground, and starts the upper-body side of your 5 kg goal.
setup: Adjust the seat so the handles line up with the middle of your chest.
Set the pin with your uninjured hand at the lightest plate.
Sit with your back flat on the pad, feet flat, shoulder blades gently pulled back.
Use the neutral (vertical) handles if the machine has them, with the handle in the heel of your hand and your wrist straight.
If there's a foot bar that moves the handles forward, use it so your arms never start in the deepest stretch.
cues: Wrists stacked over your elbows, knuckles up on horizontal handles.
Press out smoothly, exhaling, and stop just short of locking your elbows.
Shoulders stay down and back against the pad.
Take 3 s to return until your hands are just in front of your chest.
mistakes: Seat too low, so the handles sit near your shoulders. Fix: raise the seat until they're at mid-chest.
Shoulders rolling forward at the end of the press. Fix: keep your shoulder blades on the pad.
Wrists bent back. Fix: hold the handle in the heel of your palm, in line with your forearm.
Letting the stack crash. Fix: control the return.
arm_safety: After grip clearance. Ask your physio specifically about pushing. Start at the lightest plate for two weeks, then progress by the smallest step the machine allows. Choose neutral handles if there are any and keep your wrists straight. Your uninjured arm will want to do more, so keep the handles level and slow so both sides share the work. Arm rule: stay within your physio's pain limit (if you haven't been given one, 2/10 or less during the set), settled by the next morning, no new swelling. Any ache at the fracture site means drop the weight. Fall risk is low. Sit down and stand up using your legs, with your uninjured hand on the frame.
dose: First fortnight: 3 × 10–12, RIR 3. Then 3 × 8–12, RIR 2–3. Add one plate when every set reaches 12.

name: Dumbbell bench press
why: Each arm works on its own, so your uninjured arm can't cover for the injured one, and you can choose the wrist angle that feels best. It's a reliable chest and arm builder for your muscle goal.
setup: Sit on the end of a flat bench with the dumbbells standing on your thighs near your knees.
Lie back slowly, holding the dumbbells close to your chest as you go. Don't kick them up with a jerk.
Feet flat, shoulder blades gently pulled back and down, a slight natural arch.
Start with your palms facing each other (neutral) or turned slightly in.
cues: Wrists straight, stacked over your elbows.
Elbows about 45° from your sides, not flared to 90°.
Press up and slightly in as you exhale.
Take 3 s to lower the dumbbells until they're beside your chest.
mistakes: Dumbbells drifting out wide, so your shoulders ache. Fix: tuck your elbows to about 45° and shorten the range.
Wrists bending back. Fix: grip the middle of the handle and keep it over your forearm.
Dropping the dumbbells out to the sides at the end. Fix: bring them to your chest, then sit up with them resting on your thighs.
Arms moving unevenly. Fix: slow down so both sides move together.
arm_safety: After grip clearance, and after a few weeks of machine chest press without arm symptoms. Dumbbells need balancing as well as pushing, so start lighter than you think (4–6 kg each) with a neutral grip, equal weights and your injured side setting the load. Getting into and out of position is the riskiest part. Lie back with the dumbbells held to your chest, and at the end bring them back to your chest and sit up with them on your thighs. Never drop them out to the sides. Arm rule: stay within your physio's pain limit (if you haven't been given one, 2/10 or less during the set), settled by the next morning, no new swelling. Fall risk is low.
dose: 3 × 8–12 (6–10 in Phase 3), RIR 2–3. Add 2 kg per hand when every set reaches the top of the range.

name: Barbell bench press
equipment: bench press station with safety arms, or a flat bench inside a squat rack with safeties
why: The benchmark upper-body press, and the last step of your push progression. It lets you add load in small steps for years. It also creates less pressure inside your trunk than squats and deadlifts, which makes it a sensible first barbell press after the injury.
setup: Lie with your eyes directly under the bar. Set the safety arms just below your chest height with your chest lifted, and check them with the empty bar.
Grip slightly wider than your shoulders with your thumbs wrapped round the bar (never thumbless). The bar sits low in your palm, over your forearm.
Pull your shoulder blades back and down into the bench, feet flat, a slight natural arch.
Lift the bar off the hooks with straight arms and bring it over your shoulders. Ask for a spotter to hand it to you if you can.
cues: Wrists straight: knuckles up, bar over your forearm bones.
Lower to your lower chest in 2–3 s, elbows at 45–70°.
Press up and slightly back towards the rack as you exhale.
Keep your bum on the bench and your feet planted.
mistakes: Wrists bent back. Fix: move the bar down to the heel of your palm.
Elbows flared to 90°. Fix: tuck them a little so the bar touches lower on your chest.
Bouncing the bar off your chest. Fix: touch, then press.
Benching without safety arms. Fix: always set them. If a rep stalls, lower the bar to your chest and onto the arms, then slide out.
arm_safety: Full clearance only (your plan brings it in at Phase 4), after many weeks of pain-free dumbbell pressing. The bar makes both hands share the load, so a weaker injured side shows up as a tilting bar. Keep it light enough that the bar stays level. Start with the empty 20 kg bar, or stay with dumbbells if that's too much, then add 1.25–2.5 kg a side per session. Your wrists must stay straight with the bar over your forearm bones. Arm rule: stay within your physio's pain limit (if you haven't been given one, 2/10 or less during the set), settled by the next morning, no new swelling. Fall risk is low, but getting stuck under the bar is a real risk, so always set the safety arms or have a spotter.
dose: 3 × 5–8, RIR 2–3. Empty bar first. Add 2.5 kg in total per session while the bar moves smoothly.

name: Incline push-up
equipment: Smith machine bar locked at chest-to-hip height, or a barbell in a rack, or a bench wedged against a wall
why: The bridge from wall presses to floor push-ups: bodyweight pressing with a braced trunk and shoulder blades that move freely. Push-up strength helps you get up off the ground, scramble, and catch yourself if you stumble.
setup: Lock a Smith or rack bar at chest-to-hip height. The higher the bar, the easier the push-up.
Hold the bar with your hands slightly wider than your shoulders, then walk your feet back until your body is a straight line.
Squeeze your glutes and quads and keep your ribs down: it's a plank on a slope.
cues: Your body moves as one piece, a plank that bends at the elbows.
Elbows at about 45°, forearms vertical.
Take 2–3 s to lower your chest to the bar, then exhale as you push away.
At the top, push the bar away so your shoulder blades spread.
mistakes: Hips sagging. Fix: squeeze your glutes, or raise the bar.
Elbows flared to 90°. Fix: tuck them to about 45°.
Half reps. Fix: chest to the bar every rep, and raise the bar if you can't reach it.
Using a bench that can slide. Fix: wedge it against a wall or use a locked Smith bar.
arm_safety: Full clearance only, because this puts bodyweight through your wrists. Holding a bar keeps your wrists straight, which is usually kinder than flat palms on a bench. Start high, with the bar at chest height, once your physio-graded wall presses feel easy. Lower the bar one notch at a time over weeks. Arm rule: stay within your physio's pain limit (if you haven't been given one, 2/10 or less during the set), settled by the next morning, no new swelling. Fall risk is low. Set the bar high enough that if your hands slip, you can step forward and stand.
dose: 3 × 6–12, RIR 2–3. Lower the bar one notch when 3 × 12 is easy with a perfect plank.

name: Push-up
equipment: optional: fixed hexagonal dumbbells to hold, keeping your wrists straight
why: A pressing standard you can do anywhere, and a whole-body plank in motion. StrongFirst-style crisp sets build pressing strength without grinding.
setup: Place your hands just wider than your shoulders and under them, fingers spread. Or grip fixed hex dumbbells to keep your wrists straight.
Feet together or hip-width, body straight from ears to ankles.
Squeeze your glutes and quads, brace your trunk and pull your shoulders away from your ears.
cues: Screw your hands into the floor so your elbows point back.
Lower as one unit until your chest is a fist's height from the floor.
Elbows about 45° from your body.
Push the floor away as you exhale.
Stop the set while every rep still looks the same.
mistakes: Hips sagging or piking up. Fix: squeeze your glutes and film yourself from the side.
Head dipping first. Fix: tuck your chin and let your chest lead.
Elbows flared out. Fix: tuck them to 45°.
Grinding sets to failure. Fix: do sets of 3–8 well short of failure, and add sets for more volume.
arm_safety: Full clearance only. Flat-palm push-ups bend your wrists back close to their limit under a large share of your bodyweight. Earn them through physio wall presses and incline push-ups at gradually lower heights. If wrist extension still aches, hold fixed hex dumbbells (they don't roll) so your wrists stay straight. Arm rule: stay within your physio's pain limit (if you haven't been given one, 2/10 or less during the set), settled by the next morning, no new swelling. Otherwise go back to incline push-ups. Fall risk is low.
dose: 3 × 6–12, RIR 2, stopping before your form would break. Add a rep per set each week.

name: Dumbbell shoulder press (seated)
why: Overhead strength for lifting a rucksack onto your back or a bag onto a shelf, and healthy shoulders for get-ups later. Seated with your back supported is the safest way to press overhead again.
setup: Set the bench upright at 80–90° and sit with your back against it, feet flat.
Rest the dumbbells on your thighs, then bring them to your shoulders one at a time.
Palms facing each other or slightly forward, wrists straight over your elbows.
cues: Ribs down, back against the pad. Don't arch.
Press up and slightly in as you exhale, finishing with your biceps by your ears.
Take 2–3 s to lower to just below chin height.
Forearms vertical throughout.
mistakes: Arching away from the pad. Fix: brace, ribs down, go lighter.
Wrists bent back under the dumbbell. Fix: stack it over your forearm.
Pressing out in front of you. Fix: finish over your shoulders.
Dropping the dumbbells at the end. Fix: lower them to your thighs.
arm_safety: After grip clearance. Ask your physio about holding weights overhead. Start with 2–4 kg, a neutral grip and only two sets, with the same weight both sides, set by your injured arm. Bring the dumbbells up one at a time from your thighs and lower them back to your thighs at the end. Arm rule: stay within your physio's pain limit (if you haven't been given one, 2/10 or less during the set), settled by the next morning, no new swelling. Fall risk is low because you're seated with your back supported.
dose: 3 × 8–12, RIR 2–3. Add 1–2 kg per hand when every set reaches 12.

name: Triceps rope pushdown
why: Simple arm work for your muscle goal, plus the lockout strength you'll use for pressing and planting trekking poles. The rope lets your wrists sit in a natural, neutral position.
setup: Clip the rope to the top pulley with your uninjured hand and choose the lightest plate.
Stand close and grip the rope ends with your thumbs up and your elbows pinned to your sides.
Hinge forward very slightly and brace.
cues: Elbows stay glued to your ribs.
Push down and slightly apart as you exhale.
Pause with your arms straight, then let the rope rise for 2–3 s until your forearms pass horizontal.
mistakes: Elbows drifting forward, so it turns into a press. Fix: pin them and go lighter.
Leaning over the rope to use your bodyweight. Fix: stand tall.
Bending your wrists. Fix: keep them in line with your forearms.
arm_safety: After grip clearance. Start at the lightest plate and use small jumps. Both hands work equally, and if your injured side lags, slow down rather than letting your uninjured arm take over. Arm rule: stay within your physio's pain limit (if you haven't been given one, 2/10 or less during the set), settled by the next morning, no new swelling. Fall risk is low.
dose: 2–3 × 10–15, RIR 2. Add one small plate when every set reaches 15.

name: Lat pulldown
why: Builds the back and arm strength that pull-ups and scrambling need, with the load fully adjustable. A broad, strong back also adds visible muscle towards your 5 kg.
setup: Set the thigh pad so your legs fit snugly under it. Set the pin with your uninjured hand at the lightest plate.
Stand, reach up and take the bar or a neutral-grip handle with both hands. If the straight bar bothers your wrist, use the neutral handle.
Sit down with the handle, letting your legs and bodyweight bring it down rather than your arms.
cues: Lean back slightly (10–20°) with your chest up.
Pull your elbows down towards your back pockets and bring the bar to your upper chest.
Exhale as you pull, then pause for 1 s.
Let the bar rise over 2–3 s to a full stretch.
mistakes: Yanking the weight down with a big body swing. Fix: go lighter and keep your torso still.
Pulling the bar behind your neck. Fix: always pull to the front.
Shrugging. Fix: pull your shoulders down before your elbows bend.
Letting go so the bar flies up. Fix: stand up with the handle to return it under control.
arm_safety: After grip clearance. The start and end of each set, when you take the bar down from overhead and return it, are where people get careless. Sit down with the bar using your legs and stand up with it to return it. Use the lightest plate for the first fortnight. Neutral or close-grip handles are often kinder to a healing forearm than the wide bar. Both hands share the load equally. Arm rule: stay within your physio's pain limit (if you haven't been given one, 2/10 or less during the set), settled by the next morning, no new swelling. Fall risk is low.
dose: 3 × 8–12, RIR 2–3, 2–3 s return. Add one plate when every set reaches 12.

name: Seated cable row
equipment: seated cable row station, or a low pulley with a bench
why: Builds the upper back that keeps you upright under a rucksack for hours and balances all your pressing. The neutral V-handle suits a healing forearm.
setup: Clip on the V-handle with your uninjured hand and set the lightest plate.
Sit with your feet on the footplate and your knees slightly bent.
Reach forward to the handle by hinging from your hips with a flat back, then sit tall with your arms straight.
cues: Sit tall: chest proud, ribs down.
Pull the handle to your lower ribs with your elbows close to your body.
Squeeze your shoulder blades together for 1 s as you exhale.
Take 2–3 s to straighten your arms, letting your shoulder blades reach forward without your back rounding.
mistakes: Rocking back and forth to move the weight. Fix: keep your torso still and use a lighter plate.
Shrugging up to your ears. Fix: shoulders down, elbows back.
Rounding your lower back to reach the handle. Fix: hinge from your hips and bend your knees more.
arm_safety: After grip clearance. Reaching for the handle and putting it back are the moments a healing forearm gets jerked, so take and release it with both hands while the stack is resting. Start with the lightest plate, both hands equal, wrists straight. Arm rule: stay within your physio's pain limit (if you haven't been given one, 2/10 or less during the set), settled by the next morning, no new swelling. Fall risk is low. Get on and off the seat using your legs.
dose: 3 × 8–12, RIR 2–3. Add one plate when every set reaches 12.

name: Machine row (chest-supported)
why: The chest pad takes your lower back out of the movement, so you can focus on your upper back in the most stable set-up possible. It's a good first two-handed pull after grip clearance.
setup: Adjust the seat so the handles are level with your lower chest, and set the chest pad so you can just reach them with straight arms.
Set the pin with your uninjured hand at the lightest plate.
Choose the neutral (vertical) handles if there are any.
cues: Chest stays on the pad.
Lead with your elbows and pull them past your ribs.
Squeeze for 1 s as you exhale, then return over 2–3 s.
mistakes: Chest coming off the pad. Fix: go lighter.
Shrugging. Fix: shoulders down first, then row.
Short, jerky reps. Fix: full stretch forward, full squeeze back.
